In brief

In the novel's cast of hundreds of people, most of them "real" to some extent, one small off-stage role is played by a woman whom Mulligan calls simply "the aunt." Oliver St. John Gogarty had five aunts, but only one of them, Miss Annie Oliver, was a member of his nuclear family. In June 1904 she was 53 years old and may well have resided at the Gogartys' home at 5 Rutland Square, helping to take charge of the family while her sister Margaret wrestled with severe illness.

At more length

In an essay on James Joyce Online Notes, Harald Beck examines the possible real-life models for Mulligan's aunt and rules out all but one. Doctor Henry Gogarty, Oliver's father, had a sister but she married in 1867 and immediately emigrated to New York. His wife Margaret, née Oliver, had four sisters. Two of them, Sarah and Delia, had permanently entered religious orders. Julia married in 1877 and petitioned for divorce in 1888. Annie Oliver, born in Galway on 4 October 1849, administered her father's will after his death in 1885 and apparently moved to Dublin several years later. After her brother-in-law's death in 1891 she lived in the house on Rutland Square, helping her sister raise Oliver, Henry, Richard, and Mary Florence. Newspaper reports indicate that the two sisters did charitable work at various bazaars during those years. The 1901 census shows that Annie had moved to a boarding house for women at 10 Gardiner Street, but soon after that Margaret began to suffer from the bronchitis and emphysema that killed her in 1906, so it is entirely possible, Beck infers, that Annie moved back into the house on Rutland Square to help care for her and her children.

These details are consistent with Mulligan's remarks about "the aunt," which portray her as a quasi-parental controlling force in the family household. In Telemachus he says to Stephen, "We must go to Athens. Will you come if I can get the aunt to fork out twenty quid?" Later he remarks, "The aunt thinks you killed your mother [...] That's why she won't let me have anything to do with you." And still later in the chapter: "The aunt always keeps plainlooking servants for Malachi. Lead him not into temptation." A woman who chooses the family servants, doles out significant sums of money, and decides on children's choice of friends must be reckoned something more than just a visiting relative.

The impression of a close relative acting in loco parentis is reinforced by references in three later chapters. In Proteus Stephen recalls the remark about the aunt wanting to separate the two young men ("The aunt thinks you killed your mother. That's why she won't let me have anything to do with you") and then breaks into a verse from a rousing Percy French ballad about an aunt who "keeps things decent" in the family. In Scylla and Charybdis Mulligan indicates that his aunt is preparing to act on her resolution: "The aunt is going to call on your unsubstantial father." In Oxen of the Sun the threatened visit to the Dedalus home has turned into an epistolary attack: "Aunty mine's writing Pa Kinch. Baddybad Stephen lead astray goodygood Malachi."

Harald Beck quotes from two of Oliver Gogarty's autobiographical memoirs to suggest that he regarded Annie as snobbish, upper-crusty, and controlling. In Tumbling in the Hay (1939) he writes, "But when a fellow has an aunt who knows all about the Royal Family and half the Almanac de Gotha by heart. And, when we have turkey, goose or gunnard for dinner calls the stuffing 'the concealment', what is a fellow to do?" (116). In It Isn't This Time of Year At All (1954) he cites her disapproval of his bicycle racing: "'God has blessed you with a robust body. Youth must find an outlet for its energy. If you can spare the time from your studies, you might join the Ward Union Hunt'" (47).

Ulick O'Connor's biography of Gogarty describes his mother as beautiful, energetic, garrulous, smart, and funny (14). It would seem that "the aunt" did not fare very well in his comparison. But both women were opinionated, strong agents, and they seem to have acted as a team in some ways. Two surviving letters of Margaret Gogarty suggest that she was just as concerned about Joyce's influence on her son as Annie was, and just as determined to do something about it.

John Hunt 2026
